title: Senior's toolkit: reading, minting and validating JWTs
summary: Decode a token in the shell or jwt.ms, mint test tokens with dotnet user-jwts, and validate with JsonWebTokenHandler and the right parameters.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: reading, minting and validating JWTs
steps.body: When an API says 401, the first question is always "what is in the token?". These are the ways experienced developers read a token, make one for local testing, and configure validation so it checks what matters.

toolkit.what: Read a JWT's payload in the shell: take the middle part, turn base64url into base64, add the missing `=` padding, decode. Nothing leaves your machine.
flags: base64url uses `-` and `_` where base64 uses `+` and `/`

toolkit.what: Microsoft's token decoder: paste a token and see its header and claims explained. It decodes in the browser, but treat real production tokens as secrets anyway: they are live credentials until they expire.
flags: each claim with a short explanation

toolkit.what: Mint a signed token for local development that your API's JwtBearer setup accepts. It writes the signing key to user secrets and the issuer and audience to `appsettings.Development.json`.
flags: the user name in the token
add a role claim (repeat for more)
toolkit.example:
dotnet user-jwts create --name ana --role admin --scope "tasks:write"
dotnet user-jwts list
dotnet user-jwts print <id> --show-all
toolkit.when: testing protected endpoints without a real identity provider

toolkit.what: Call the API with a token and read the answer. On a 401 the `WWW-Authenticate` header often says why.
flags: everything, including the request headers curl sent

toolkit.what: The current .NET token validator (package `Microsoft.IdentityModel.JsonWebTokens`), used by JwtBearer itself. It returns a result instead of throwing.
flags: true only if signature, issuer, audience and lifetime all pass
why it failed (IDX error code inside)
toolkit.example:
var result = await new JsonWebTokenHandler().ValidateTokenAsync(token, parameters);
if (!result.IsValid) logger.LogWarning(result.Exception, "Token rejected");

toolkit.what: What validation checks. Set the issuer, audience and the algorithms you expect, never fewer.
flags: the key, or keys from JWKS via `Authority`

steps.prompt: Match each part of the shell decode to its job.
pairs: take the payload between the two dots
put back the padding base64url removed
decode the bytes to JSON text

steps.prompt: A token whose `exp` was 3 minutes ago is still accepted by your API. A tester files a bug. What explains it?
options: `ClockSkew` defaults to 5 minutes, so tokens are accepted up to 5 minutes past `exp`; lower it if that matters
The API does not check `exp` at all
`exp` is measured in minutes, not seconds
steps.explain: Clock skew allows for servers whose clocks drift apart. Five minutes is generous; many teams set 30 seconds to 2 minutes, which still covers normal drift.

steps.prompt: Mint a local token for user `ana` with the `admin` role, then call the API with it.
Every call returns 401 and the log says the following. What do you check first?
steps.code: IDX10214: Audience validation failed. Audiences: 'api://orders'. Did not match: validationParameters.ValidAudience: 'api://tasks' or validationParameters.ValidAudiences: 'null'.
options: The token was issued for `api://orders`, not for this API: request a token for `api://tasks` (or fix `ValidAudience` if the API's name really changed)
The user lacks the admin role
steps.explain: IDX10214 is audience, IDX10223 is lifetime (expired), and signature problems are IDX10503 or IDX10511-style messages. Decode the token and compare `aud` with what the API expects.

steps.prompt: Safe validation setting, or a hole?
items: `ValidateAudience = false` because the audience kept failing
steps.explain: Turning a check off to make a 401 go away hides the bug and opens the door: any token from that issuer, for any API, at any time, or not signed at all.

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: On any 401, decode the token first and compare `iss`, `aud`, `exp` and the claims with what the API expects; the IDX code in the log tells you which check failed. Use `dotnet user-jwts` for local tests, and never fix a validation failure by switching the check off.
